blocks.text: Quick verdict

Rayobyte is the better value for most scraping budgets: $35 for 10 GB against $80 on Oxylabs pay-as-you-go, around $200 for 100 GB, $0.90/GB at a terabyte against Oxylabs' best $2.50/GB, and traffic that never expires. Oxylabs is the better choice for hardened targets and enterprise pipelines that need the largest pool, SOCKS5 (Rayobyte's residential gateway is HTTP(S) only), ZIP and ASN targeting, scraper APIs and formal sourcing documentation. Price-led teams should start with Rayobyte.

Oxylabs and Rayobyte both sell residential, datacenter, ISP and mobile proxies, and both have deep datacenter heritage, but they sit at opposite ends of the price scale. Oxylabs is a premium enterprise vendor with a 175M+ residential pool, published 99.95% success rates and per-result scraper APIs. Rayobyte is a US-based value provider whose non-expiring residential traffic falls to $0.90/GB at a terabyte. This comparison works out when Oxylabs' quality is worth paying for.

blocks.text: Oxylabs in 2026: what you get

Oxylabs is a Lithuanian web-data company and Bright Data's closest rival at the top of the market. It advertises a residential pool of more than 175 million IPs across 195 locations, publishes a 99.95% success rate for residential traffic, and sells seven product lines including datacenter, ISP and mobile proxies, a Web Scraper API and Web Unblocker. Onboarding is more sales-led than the mid-market providers, but self-service has expanded through 2026, including dedicated ISP proxies.

Strengths: One of the two largest residential pools available; Published 99.95% residential success rate; Strong scraper APIs that bill per result; Formal ethical-sourcing documentation for procurement. Weak spots: Expensive at low volume ($8/GB PAYG); Best rates need large monthly commitments; Residential trial goes through sales rather than self-service.
Rayobyte in 2026: what you get

Rayobyte is a US proxy company that started life as Blazing SEO and built its name on dedicated datacenter proxies. Residential proxies have since become its main product. It sells them pay-as-you-go in four volume bands with traffic that never expires, sources at least part of its residential pool in-house, and offers country, region and city targeting. The notable limit is protocol support: its residential gateway does not support SOCKS5 or UDP.

Strengths: Non-expiring residential traffic; Steep volume discounts down to $0.90/GB; Excellent datacenter and ISP catalog; Well-regarded human support. Weak spots: No SOCKS5 or UDP on residential; Pool size not prominently published; Fewer advanced targeting options than enterprise providers.
Pricing: Oxylabs vs Rayobyte

Oxylabs charges $8/GB pay-as-you-go for residential traffic. Monthly plans start with Starter at $30 for 5 GB ($6/GB) and a Basic tier around $100 for 20 GB, and the rate falls to $2.50/GB on the $2,500/month Corporate plan. Mobile traffic starts at $7.50/GB.
Rayobyte prices residential traffic in four pay-as-you-go bands: $3.50/GB for 1-49 GB, $2/GB for 50-249 GB, $1.50/GB for 250-999 GB and $0.90/GB for 1-5 TB. Traffic does not expire.

Buying 10 GB, you would pay about $35 with Rayobyte and $80 with Oxylabs: a 56% saving in Rayobyte's favour. At 100 GB, a like-for-like total is harder to state because Oxylabs does not publish an exact price for that volume; Rayobyte comes to about $200. Look past the per-GB figure too. Rayobyte lets unused traffic carry forward, while Oxylabs's allowance does not (monthly plan allowances reset each cycle). For irregular workloads, that difference can outweigh a small gap in list price.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

Rayobyte does not publish a clear residential pool figure, so a size comparison is not possible on published data. Oxylabs lists '175M+' and Rayobyte lists 'Not prominently published'. In practice, what matters is how many unique IPs you get in the countries you target, which you can measure in a short trial by sending a few thousand requests and counting distinct exit addresses. For coverage, Oxylabs lists 195 countries and Rayobyte lists Global. On targeting, Oxylabs offers country, state, city, ZIP and ASN, while Rayobyte offers country, region and city.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Protocol support is a real difference here. Oxylabs supports HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS5, while Rayobyte offers HTTP, HTTPS (no SOCKS5 on residential). If your tooling needs SOCKS5, for example some anti-detect browsers, desktop apps or non-HTTP traffic, that settles it in Oxylabs's favour. On sessions, Oxylabs offers rotating and sticky sessions on residential and mobile, and Rayobyte offers rotates per request by default; sticky sessions available. Setup works the same way on both: a single gateway endpoint, with location and session options passed as username parameters, plus IP whitelisting if you prefer not to use credentials.
Which is better for your use case?
General web scraping: Oxylabs. Oxylabs has the edge here. Why: its pool size and Web Scraper API suit large crawls. How Rayobyte compares: cheap volume bands and traffic that never expires.
SERP and rank tracking: Oxylabs. Oxylabs has the edge here. Why: its scraper API returns parsed search results. How Rayobyte compares: usable, with no dedicated SERP product.

Social media and multi-account management: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With Oxylabs: it works, but the pricing is built for volume, not a handful of accounts. With Rayobyte: no SOCKS5 limits some account tools. Run the same small test on both before committing.

E-commerce price and stock monitoring: Oxylabs. Oxylabs has the edge here. Why: city and ZIP targeting plus parsed e-commerce endpoints. How Rayobyte compares: city targeting and low prices at volume.
Ad verification and geo-testing: Oxylabs. Oxylabs has the edge here. Why: broad geo coverage with ASN targeting. How Rayobyte compares: fewer carrier or ASN controls.
Tight budgets: Rayobyte wins. The deciding factor for Rayobyte: $2/GB from 50 GB and $0.90/GB at a terabyte. The limitation on the Oxylabs side: entry pricing is among the highest in this comparison.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. Oxylabs: Residential trial arranged through sales, once per customer. Rayobyte: Check current offer. Verification and payment rules differ too. Oxylabs: Business verification on larger accounts. Rayobyte: Standard verification; US company. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test Oxylabs and Rayobyte before you commit
Spec sheets only get you so far. A short, structured test on your own targets will settle Oxylabs vs Rayobyte faster than any review:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (Oxylabs: residential trial arranged through sales, once per customer; Rayobyte: check current offer).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, Oxylabs comes out ahead in 4, Rayobyte in 1, and 1 is a tie. That makes Oxylabs the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: Oxylabs is strongest for large scraping pipelines with steady volume, while Rayobyte is strongest for mid-to-high volume scraping on a budget. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
